speechtext:
Just before that motion is
adopted, there are a few remarks I should like to make, especially since it was on my motion that the inquiry was made before the banking and commerce committee. I do not desire to move an amendment to that report, which like all reports, is more or less of a compromise, but I should like to point out very briefly some of the facts which came before this committee which are not enibodied in the report..
While undoubtedly the attention of the committee was centered upon the suggestion of a central bank of issue and rediscount at the same time there were other suggestions made, such as the establishment of small local banks, and the possibility of setting up cooperative credit societies. These matters were not gone into by your committee.
Futher than that, there were a- number of general criticisms advanced with regard to the present banking system. The witnesses that came before the committee were, with one exception, either officials of the department or else those connected with the Canadian Bankers Association. Under these circumstances we had not the opportunity of considering as many of these criticisms as personally I should have liked. I am not blaming the committee; the trouble lay in the fact that very few business men cared to come forward to criticize the banks. I do not know whether their objections are well taken but while privately they criticize the banks, they express themselves as afraid to come forward publicly lest their credit should be interfered with. I do not know whether those fears are justified; I merely mention that for what it is worth.
In rebuttal of various criticisms which were made, the bankers made claims which I summarize as follows:
(a)	That the small number of banks in Canada (four banks controlling approximately 70 per cent of the entire deposits) is in the interests of Canada.
(b)	That according to the banks' code of honour, in the granting of credits there is no discrimination against a business concern that is a rival to one in which a bank director is also a director.
(c)	That on the contrary, interlocking directorates are a distinct advantage.
(d)	That districts remote from headquarters are under no disadvantage.
(e)	That it is not the function of a bank to take the hazards of the commencement of a manufacturing business but that any solvent concern in a liquid shape can obtain all the cerdit it can reasonably desire for legitimate purposes.

No legitimate loan properly secured has been refused from one end of Canada to the other, since I have been a banker.

I have read the report sent out by

What happened was this: On April 9 Chief Justice Meredith wrote a letter to the Under-Secretary of State, Mr. Mulvey, which I will now read:
My dear Mr. Mulvey:
The same question in regard to naturalization in Canada of aliens, about which I had some correspondence with you a while ago, has arisen again, in the same place and in regard to the same class of persons.
The still unsatisfactory state of the law and the practice under the act has impelled me to put in writing some thoughts on the subject in the hope that they may lead to something being done to put the matter on a better footing.

The enclosed paper is merely a draft. I have done nothing yet.
On April 17 of this year the Under-Secretary of State replied as follows:
My dear Judge Meredith:
Your letter of the 9th arrived during my absence from Ottawa. I am very glad indeed to have your opinion upon the subjects therein touched upon in respect of the naturalization of aliens. This will be of great assistance to the Secretary of State in promoting a bill which is at present before parliament for the purpose of amending the Naturalization Act, eliminating the clauses winch require applicants for naturalization to be heard by a judge. I agree with your view throughout. In fact, I have for years been trying to prevail upon the Secretary of State to put forw'ard the bill which is now under consideration.

My hon. friend's interruption shows that I was right in saying that I should again direct the attention of the committee to the main principle of the act, which principle the leader of the opposition has lost sight of. Under the present system the Secretary of State, representing the government of Canada, can pass on naturalization papers only where the judiciary have pronounced favourably on the application, and the purpose of the bill is to bring the applicants directly before the Secretary of State and to vest in him full discretion under certain regulations to grant naturalization certificates.
I am sure my hon. friend does not desire to make any misstatement of facts.
No.

Section 4 of the act, which is the principal section determining the conditions under which naturalization shall be granted, contains subsection 3, which is the present law, but which the Minister of Railways was so persistent a moment ago in saying that it was not so. Subsection 3 reads:
Naturalization Act

The grant of a certificate of naturalization to any such alien shall be in the absolute discretion of the minister and he may, with or without assigning any reason, give or withhold the certificate as he thinks most conducive to the public good, and no appeal shall lie from his decision.
That section is a standard section throughout the empire. It was drafted by British draftsmen; it is the law of Canada to-day and it will continue to be unless my hon. friend takes it out of the statute. This subsection is not touched by this amendment.

If my hon. friend will
refer to my first statement in the house, he will see that I have been contending right along that this section was the underlying principle of our act.
Of all acts.

I was basing my appeal
to the house on that subsection. I am glad to see my hon. friend admits at last that the subsection is the underlying principle of our act, because that is what I have been contending all the time. What I have endeavoured to demonstrate to the committee and the country is that the sections that we desire to repeal are inconsistent with that very subsection which I have read and which my hon. friend has just read. If my hon. friend will refer to my speech of last Monday, he will find that my first argument was that the principle of the legislation was included in the subsection which he has just read and that sections 22 to 27 inclusive which we wish to repeal are inconsistent with that subsection. In the other British dominions the Secretary of State has, in conformity with what has just been read, and under certain regulations, absolute discretion in regard to granting certificates. When the applications come to him he has absolute discretion to dispose of them one way or the other, provided that the regulations have been followed.
So he has in Canada.
In this country, becaus'e of the existence of the sections which we now propose to repeal, the Secretary of State can exercise that discretion only when the courts have reported favourably.
No. It does not say so. It says the opposite.
Then there will be no reason for objecting to my bill.
The objection to the bill was largely because the minister was taking away the discretion altogether from the courts and vesting it in the Secretary of State.
The leader of the opposition seems to contend that this is the law now.
So it is and has been ever since the statute has been on the statute books.
I would feel like putting a question to my hon. friend now. Does he claim that under the present law the Secretary of State has absolute discretion in the granting of naturalization?
Absolutely.
Then why obj ect to this bill?
Because it abolishes the safeguard of a judicial inquiry.

This conference approves the scheme of imperial citizenship based on the following five propositions:
These are the five propositions that he gave:
1.	Imperial nationality should be world-wide and uniform, each dominion being left free to grant local nationality on such terms as its legislature thinks fit.
2.	The mother country finds it necessary to maintain five years as a qualifying period. This is a safeguard to the dominions as well
as to us, but five years anywhere in the empire should be as good as five years in the United Kingdom.
3.	The grant of nationality is in every case discretionary and this discretion should be exercised by those responsible in the area in which the applicant has spent the last twelve months.
4.	The imperial act should be so framed as to enable each self-governing dominion to adopt it.
5.	Nothing now proposed (this again is not necessary but only to make clear where we stand-it is only an "aide memoire") would affect the validity and effectiveness of local law regulating immigration and the like or differentiating between the classes of British subjects.

of certificates-the number for that year being 797-which are merely renewals of certificates that had. been granted under the old act previous to 1914. Well, I fancy our friends opposite will agree that in this regard the Secretary of State is in the same position as are other ministers of the crown. Do hon. gentlemen suppose that the Minister of Public Works supervises in person every public work in the country, or that the Minister of National Revenue is present at every port of entry to find out personally whether the customs regulations are properly observed, or that the Minister of Immigration interviews every immigrant coming into the country and, in person, makes sure that the regulations are lived up to? Every minister in this government or in any other government that has existed in the country is in the same situation. The minister lays down his policy and is responsible for the administration of the act, but he does not deni personally with every case appertaining to his department. Of course, he has a staff; he has an organized body of officers to do this work. In my opinion, the whole machinery of responsible government rests upon the fact that the government of which the minister is a member defines the policy, he is responsible for the administration of his department, and parliament exercises control over the manner in which any act has been administered as well as over the policy that has been defined by the government. That is the complete machinery which is at the command of every responsible government. I do not see why suddenly these fears should manifest themselves, that in the case of naturalization, unless the Secretary of State deals personally with every case that is brought to his notice, the act cannot be carried out at all. I say, what the Secretary of State is responsible for is the policy of his department and the proper administration of that policy by his officers. There is nothing extraordinary in this; it is 
the condition that exists in every department of the public service.
My hon. friends have pointed out that in the other dominions the regulations, such as we enforce in the Department of the Secretary of State, are made statutory. I had indicated when introducing the bill the way in which the department intended to proceed with these cases if we did away with the reference to the courts. I may observe, however, that I am broadminded enough to accept a suggestion when I think it is good, and I admit that there is some force in the argument for making the regulations statutory instead of leaving them to be drawn up by whoever happens to be in charge of the department. There is something in that argument, and I contend that, we are giving a proof of our willingness to accept sound suggestions, a proof that we have no improper motive in putting through the bill, when we say that we are perfectly ready to accept the proposal and to make some of the essential regulations statutory. My hon. friend has been good enough-and I want to thank him for it-to point out the statutory regulations in force in the different dominions of the empire. He quoted from the Newfoundland statute, from the New Zealand statute and from the statutes of South Africa and of Australia. If hon. members have read the speech carefully, or if they heard it- and I may say that I paid the greatest attention to it myself-they wall find that all these regulations embodied in statutes in the different dominions touch certain points and provide certain safeguards. They have to do with the proper notice of the application which must be given; they deal with the delay which must ensue after the application is filed before the certificate is granted, and they also touch the question of the testimony which may be forwarded with the application in order to make it easier for the department to appreciate the qualifications of the applicant. I have gone through these statutes and have convinced myself that in the different dominions all the regulations which art statutory cover the points which I have just indicated. That is the reason why, in my desire to make our act as strongly British as possible, to follow the practice which exists throughout the British Empire as closely as we can while providing at the same time what we believe should lie within the discretion of the government in a matter of this kind in order to give the country the greatest safeguards possible in the granting of certificates, I have decided to propose further amendments to the com-

mittee which will make statutory those regulations which it had been our intention at first to leave to the department as they are left at present. In the first place, an applicant will be required to advertise his intention to seek naturalization, in a newspaper published at or nearest to his place of residence, in either the English or the French language, a copy of which advertisement must be furnished to the minister. In the second place we are asking the applicant to have his petition accompanied by certificates as to his character and his adequate knowledge of French or English from three natural born British subjects, two of whom must be householders and one a justice of the peace. The publication of these applications in newspapers is a provision which obtains in both South Africa and Australia, but in Canada we have the additional safeguard that a notice will be posted in the post office nearest the residence of the applicant. Therefore on this point we have two safeguards or guarantees as against the one which prevails in other portions of the empire. With regard to the certificates which must accompany such applications, we have gone further than the Australian statute, which provides that a certificate shall be produced from three natural born British subjects. two of whom must be householders and one a justice of the peace, a postmaster, a teacher in a state school or an officer of the police. After hearing our friends opposite claim that if a postmaster were a partisan appointed by this government he could not be entrusted even with the important function of posting an applicant in his post office, we decided that we should not include a certificate from a postmaster among those which could be accepted with the application. We desire to make it imperative that whoever applies for naturalization shall send in his application together with certificates from three natural born British subjects, two of whom must be householders and the other a justice of the peace. I trust that after the applicant has filled the form which is provided, in which he is forced to make full declaration as to his identity, the length of his stay in the country, the manner in which he entered the country, his family, his knowledge of one of the two languages, his character and so on, accompanied by the three certificates of which I have spoken, the department will have some reason to believe that the application is made in good faith.

The minister is not facile in making the best of a bad case. He is altogether too diffuse and redundant to be convincing. He has made a long explanation of the bill amending the act, but I do not think he has convinced any person who is not simply bound by party ties himself, that the proposed change is in the interest of the country or of good government.
The situation at the present is that the minister has absolute discretion in granting naturalization. Everyone will admit that it is impossible for him to investigate and that he must have some person to advise him whether or not the party applying is entitled to naturalization. Under the present act we have the most reputable and dependable people in the Dominion of Canada appointed to advise the minister. The gravamen of my complaint is that he substitutes for those dependable and reputable men all three partisans who can make a report such as they think will be in the interest of the party which is in power. If the government changes, this party will probably benefit, but until it does, that party benefits. A man who is applying for naturalization will have, so long as party politics are what they are in this country, no trouble in getting three native-born Canadians to vouch for him. In the western provinces there has not been a Conservative government since 1905, so that every justice of the peace in Alberta and Saskatchewan and many in Manitoba are appointees of the Liberal party and whatever justice of the peace we have to sign these papers in those provinces will foe a partisan, a man who has been given that dignity because of his services to the party.
Does the same thing not apply to judges?

I do not think so. I know judges are appointed partly for political considerations, but the responsibility imposed upon them leads them to act more carefully and judicially after they have been appointed than they would do before. The traditions

of the bench, are such as to have great influence on a man after he is appointed, no matter by what party. The judiciary of Canada maintains a high standard and every member of it, whether he is a county or high court judge, is keen to maintain the best traditions of the position. A justice of the peace, who is a partisan appointee, could easily dig up others of the same stripe, and whether the man was qualified or not, whether he could speak English or French, whether he had been five years in the country or whether he had the other qualifications or not, if the justice of peace lacked that sense of responsibility which is inherent in the judges he would send on that man's application. I am surprised that any body of responsible public men, having due regard for their reputations in the public service, would introduce a bill of this character into the House of Commons. They Me open before the country to the charge of making it easy, in order to perpetuate the party in power, to naturalize men who are not qualified for naturalization. I do not suppose many hon. gentlemen opposite would resort to any practices of that kind, but at election time there are men who are not altogether of the type of the men who sit on the other side. We have the Baldy Robb case. We have not forgotten the "thin red line" in Manitoba during *fhe Sifton regime, when thousands if not tens of thousands of men who had been in that province for many years were struck off the list simply by having a thin red line run through their names. I would have been against
this bill as originally introduced on account of some of the objections that have been raised, but with the amendments I think it meets all the objections that are reasonable. It has been stated again and again that even if it costs a little more, it would be worth while for the privilege of becoming a British subject. But it costs, not a little more, but a great deal more. I can see the point of view of hon. members who represent cities, because there is no necessity for this act in the city. It is in the country districts that it is needed, and there is a good deal of country in Canada which deserves consideration in connection with this matter. It is very expensive and in many cases the expense is prohibitive, for an alien to get naturalized. It is all very well to say that a judge goes around. The judge goes around one or two centres, and you cannot get him to go anywhere else. Let me quote one particular case. The county court judge who is going to sit at a particular place notifies the registrar perhaps ten days before he is coming, or perhaps, two weeks. There are people in that district who want to go to that court to be naturalized, but they receive their mail only once a month, or perhaps twice, and by the time they receive the notification from the registrar it is too late to get to the court. Or the steamer may take a little longer than was expected and the applicant may not reach the court in time, and he has to come back again in three months. The cost of all that to an alien, to poor people living in out-of-the way places, is enormous. It has cost a man $200 to get naturalized. The average alien is not too ready to get naturalized, and he should be encouraged, rather than discouraged, in a reasonable way, at any rate, and it is for that reason that I am supporting this bill.
A great deal has been made by hon. gentlemen opposite of the better ability which the judiciary have for sizing up a man's qualifications for citizenship. They say that a judge is trained to weigh evidence, and so on. Perhaps he is better trained to do that

than men working in very different positions, but what opportunity does the judge have to judge this man? The man comes into court. He is clean, sober, properly dressed, and carefully posted by the lawyer or agent who represents him just what to say in answer to the judge's remarks. I have done it myself.
I know the sort of questions the judge is going to ask, and I tell the 'applicant the answers he should give, and of course they are nice and proper, and he gets by with them. The ten minutes that he is before the judge is the only opportunity the judge has of finding out whether that man will make a good citizen. The roan stammers out a few words of broken English, and thinks that conditions in Russia are going a bit too far, or something of that kind, and he gets his certificate.
But under the proposed system to be carried out by the Secretary of State, the Secretary of State makes his own investigation -and after all he does it now-not personally, of course, as has been so often suggested, but generally by means of the police. Do you think, Mr. Chairman, that a policeman who goes into a little country place containing fifty people is not in a position to get the real dope, as we say, on that mans pedigree? Do you not think that a man s neighbours among whom he has lived for at least five years would be in a better position to size him up and gauge his qualifications for citizenship than the judge who sees him only for ten minutes? They know whether he beats his wife, gets drunk, and does not pay his bills, or whatever it is that characterizes an undesirable citizen. If there is anything against a man, you can surely rely upon somebody in these small places bringing it up, because there is always somebody who has more or less of a grudge against a particular man. The most cursory investigation on the ground is much better than half a dozen investigations by a judge who only sees a man for a few minutes in court.
I suppose we are discussing the whole of these amendments, Mr. Chairman. I think it would be better to take them up separately, but they are all part of section 1, and therefore I presume it is in order for me to move the following amendment which I propose to subsection 24, which now reads:
An applicant for a certificate of naturalization shall produce to the minister certificates of character and of adequate knowledge of the English or French language from three natural born British subjects, two of whom are householders and one of whom is a justice of the peace.
[Mr. Neill. 1
I propose that it read as follows:
An applicant for a certificate of naturalization shall produce to the minister certificates of character and of adequate knowledge of the English or French language from two natural born British subjects who are householders and from a justice of the peace.
The idea being that we should not require the justice of the peace to be a natural born British subject. Otherwise the clause is practically the same. I propose that amendment for two reasons. In the first place, it is very difficult and very inconvenient in some districts to get hold of a justice of the peace who is a natural bom British subject. On the Pacific coast and on the prairie there are considerable settlements of foreigners, Scandinavians, and so on, scattered up and down the coast or over the prairie. They have come in there in a block, and after a number of years residence, not less than five, they have become naturalized. It becomes necessary to have a justice of the peace in that district, and it is most suitable and convenient and proper to pick out from among these men one whose qualifications in education and character fit him for the position, rather than picking out a British born one, who perhaps may not live within fifty miles. Therefore, the custom is to appoint the best one of these men, and I would resent the suggestion that he should be placed in a different category from the British bom justice of the peace. Some hon. member opposite drew a very distinct line between the judiciary and justices of the peace. The justice of the peace is just as reputable in many cases in his own sphere as the judge, and just as free from political bias. I do not want to attack the judiciary, but I have seen a commission presided over by a judge which was a disgrace to the judiciary because of the partisan attitude taken by the judge. It is an insult to a justice of the peace who has been forty years resident in this country and twenty years a justice of the peace-I am speaking of a case within my own knowledge -without ever a shadow of reproach, to tell him now that he is not fit to certify whether or not a man is likely to become a good citizen. It is uncalled for, and it would make the law very difficult to enforce because in these small places there is only one justice of the peace, and the applicant if he could not find him there could not go to another settlement, cut off by water or mountain, and where perhaps he would not be known. It would really nullify practically all the benefits of this act if you insisted upon the jus-

tice of the peace being a natural bora British subject. Therefore, my suggestion is that certificates should be granted by two natural born British subjects and a justice of the peace.
Mr. M'ANION: Mr. Chairman, as one of those whose constituency contains a large number of people who at one time or another apply for naturalization, and having discussed the bill briefly the first time it was before us, I wish to supplement my former remarks. I submit this case amply proves the necessity of every bill being subjected to a thorough discussion. As introduced, the bill contained two very short clauses of eleven lines, counting the introductory clause; whereas to-day the Secretary of State has brought down a fairly lengthy bill of something over thirty lines, and containing two or three important departures from his first measure. In fact this does not resemble the original bill at all. The original bill conferred full powers on the Secretary of State; to him the application for naturalization had to be made, and if he chose he could immediately grant the application, as he said in reply to a question I put to him. Last week the Secretary of State amended his bill to make the period sixty days instead of forthwith. That was an improvement, although not quite satisfactory. Now he comes forward with two amendments, covering three other points: one, the applicant must advertise in the press that he has applied for naturalization; two, the applicant must get three certificates; three, the judiciary are in a sense reinstated in the form of justices of the peace. In a word, the Secretary of State has absolutely turned his original bill upside down and converted it into a new bill. I think in its new form it is considerably improved, and presumably if we continue discussing the measure for another two or three days the Secretary of State may be able to draft a bill that will be satisfactory to the people of this country.
Let me deal briefly with some of these points. In the first place, the minister objects to the measure by which in the past the judiciary dealt with the examination of applicant for naturalization. As I have said, he has to a certain extent gone back to the old conditions by availing himself of the services of justices of the peace. This being so, why not leave the judiciary to function as in the past? The outstanding objection to the bill as originally introduced was the lack of notice. Because of the frailty of all ministers, of whatever government, there is danger in the absence of sufficient notice of large numbers of people being naturalized, by the hundred
or the thousand, in certain constituencies in order to turn elections. In its original form the bill made it possible for applications to be sent in to the Secretary of State, and if he were unscrupulous enough he could accept the application immediately and allow the newly naturalized citizens to vote. Undoubtedly that could have been done. In fact, as was pointed out in the previous discussion. that has been done in the past. Twenty years ago or more I saw a member of this house get together hundreds of applicants and secure their naturalization hurriedly in time to vote, and so turn an election. In many cases those naturalized had not fulfilled the legal requirements. The change to sixty days is an improvement, but I think the period is too short. If this bill becomes law a candidate a few months before an election could get hundreds of people naturalized and secure their support, and in a tight constituency this would be sufficient to turn the election in his favour. He would simply have to get three householders, friends of his, to hand out certificates. The justice of the peace, I admit, might be a little more difficult to persuade, but every candidate, of either party, has plenty of friends, and they would say: "After all we want these people to become Canadians." That is why I submit that sixty days is too short a period. It should be lengthened. In the United States an applicant for naturalization has to give two years' notice. We are in much the same position as the United States; in that country are many immigrants who do not speak English, and we have many who do not speak English or French. Therefore it is of the utmost importance that we copy the system of a country whose conditions are similar to our own, rather than the system of a dominion whose conditions are altogether unlike ours. For instance, in Australia 99 per cent of the people are British. I think practically the same condition obtains in all the British dominions except Canada. Therefore I submit that sixty days is too short in Canada, and if the government is going to insist on the passage of this bill the period should be made at least twice as long. In fact it would be preferable to make it six months. It makes very little difference to the man who wishes to become naturalized if his application is held up for six months. This would to a large extent remove the possibility of the abuses to which I have referred.
I think those are the two big questions for us to decide, Mr. Chairman, and in deciding them we must be governed by what will benefit the country as a whole. I think the best minds in both parties wish to promote de-
Naturalization Act

cency and purity in our political life. Then let us co-operate to that end. Let us do away with this sixty-day clause, which may lead to that crookedness in elections of which we have already had far too much. I am not claiming absolute purity for the party on this side, nor do I impute every political evil to the party on the other side; but I do claim that we shall have failed in our duty if we do not so amend this bill as to lead not only to the betterment of our citizenship but of our public life. Before he proceeds further the Secretary of State should give serious consideration to the sixty-day clause with a view to extending it very substantially.

I think everyone will agree
with the leader of the opposition, Mr. Chairman, when he says in respect to this bill that no more important measure has been brought before the house this session. I am certain that the Secretary of State can have no quarrel with the discussion. It is altogether fit and proper that this measiure should be discussed, not in a spirit of acrimony, but judicially with a view to ensure that nothing shall detract in the slightest degree from the certificate of naturalization as at present granted. The duties and obligations which are implied in a certificate of naturalization should not be diminished in the slightest degree by the bill, and for that reason I propose to deal with the bill as seriously as I can and without any casual references. I am not here for the purpose of making debating capital, as seems to be the habit of some speakers; the subject is too important. When the bill was first introduced by the minister, I, like many others, viewed it with a good deal of disfavour. Had the bill in its original form come before the house for a vote I should have been compelled to vote against it, because I realized then, as I am glad the minister realizes, that some safeguards had to be inserted in it in order to make it something worth while. In its original form, as the Secretary of State introduced it, and with no amendments such as he proposes, it would have made the Secretary of State the absolute and uncontrolled judge as to whether a certificate of naturalization should be granted.
The leader of the opposition pointed out strongly and clearly the practices of the past -practices with which most members in this house are familiar, and practices which I think every member is determined shall not occur again so far as he can prevent them. We all agree, I think, that it is impossible to change human nature by act of parliament. It is possible, of course, and eom-

paratively easy to change an act of parliament. But one can imagine, if the bill had been left in its original form, what might have happened in the time of an election when the Secretary of State would have been inundated, from every political friend of his, with applications for certificates of naturalization. He would be more than human if he could refuse the solicitations of his friends. If he did refuse them his political life would not be worth a groat, and he would very soon realize, whatever his wishes might be, that political exigencies would make it so that he could not refuse applications coming to him. For that reason therefore I was glad indeed to find the Secretary of State had introduced the amendment of sixty days.
The last speaker, referring to the sixty days, complains that it is not sufficient. Perhaps it is not sufficient. I have no fixed opinion with regard to the number of days, only I would say this: I have had considerable experience with regard to naturalization throughout the west and I realize that sixty days is surely in all conscience long enough after a period of five years' probation during which the applicant has been qualifying. I make no strong point regarding the number of days, because I cannot see any danger that is likely to occur where you have other safeguards in the bill with regard to the posting of the notice, and also in connection with the inquiries that have to be made.

I would point out to my
hon. friend, as a matter of information, that in the United States the two years is not in addition to the five years; it is part of the five years as notice of intention. If we made it six months here, or a year, that time could be included in the five years.

The applicant must have resided within the country for a period of five years. He then makes his application; but he can be granted naturalization only after the five-year period. It is not at all likely that he will make his application before the end of that period, and the two months will be reckoned in addition to the five years.
The leader of the opposition clearly and correctly stated the provisions of the different acts in the different dominions-Australia, South Africa, New Zealand and Newfoundland. He then stated the conditions under which the act was framed. In the first instance, as to the principle of these various acts, he pointed out that the law was framed by British draughtsmen and the principle has been incorporated in all the bills. But there is one fundamental difference which he now

Naturalization Act
admits-and which, to be fair, I do not think he specifically denied in his original remarks *-namely, that the principle enunciated and set forth in the statutes of these different countries is also the principle that obtains in the Dominion of Canada. That principle is this, that a certificate of naturalization must be secured under section 4, which I do not wish to read. He then dealt with the question of procedure. On that question the leader of the opposition took a stand and made his strongest objection to the bill. There came to my mind several questions that might arise in relation to the matter of procedure. In the first place, will the application to the Secretary of State direct, instead of through the agency of the courts, be a retrograde step? And, particularly, will it tend to destroy the sense of value of the privilege which a certificate of naturalization is intended to convey? Can a certificate be granted more easily, with the present amendments, and with less expense to the applicant? And, if so, is it desirable that such certificate should be granted in that way and that we should expedite procedure and minimize expense? And will the certificate be granted only after the fullest inquiry is made, as at present obtains?
Now, the leader of the opposition bases his objection, first, on the effect of the principle embodied in the statute and its relation to the regulations governing procedure. I am afraid the hon. gentleman may consider me guilty of heresy when I say that I am by no means enamoured of legislation which need not necessarily go before the courts. During all my practice I have always endeavoured to keep my clients out of court. I find that 99 per cent of the people with whom I deal have a horror of the courts, and it may be that the one per cent who do like litigation are abnormal people. I have had considerable experience in obtaining certificates of naturalization, and I am bound to say that I see no particular reason why the appearance before a court adds to the value of a certificate. Most people will agree that courts of law are at best drab affairs; the atmosphere of a court is certainly not conducive to happiness, contentment or camaraderie. The hail fellow spirit is conspicuous by its absence, and my experience has been that instead of creating a feeling of citizenship and fellowship, in the granting of a certificate of naturalization, such as it might warrant, appearance in court has had indeed the very opposite effect. I have never known of any man making an application to a court who viewed with anticipatory glee his appearance there. As a matter of
fact I have always found people very much averse to appearing in court.
I was interested in hearing what the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre said with regard to the granting of certificates of naturalization. He made a suggestion, which I myself have already made, on other occasions in other places, that if it were possible to have the certificate of naturalization made the subject of some ceremonial in the country it would add greatly to the value of the certificate. The hon. member suggested citizens' day, the first of July, when it might be possible to grant certificates to all those who were entitled to naturalization. They could appear before some public forum and be granted the certificates with all the ceremonial necessary to bring home to the applicants the fact that they were obtaining something really worth while.
It seems to me that the granting of an application by the Secretary of State direct rather than through the agency of the courts is no retrograde step. It is something which each of us can support. The question that next arises in my mind is this:	Can a certificate be granted more easily, under the present bill, and with less expense to the applicant; and, if so, is it desirable to expedite procedure and minimize expense? I think everyone who has any knowledge of the subject will agree that especially in the prairie provinces the expense is almost prohibitive to a great many of the applicants. I know of men right in my own riding who are not aJble to become naturalized because they have not the money to spend; these men have come into the country in the regular way and have taken up land; they have been here five or ten years and now wish to become citizens of Canada. I know they would make good citizens, but because they have not the money they are unable to get their certificates. If this bill will reduce their expenses I think we should support it as strongly as possible, and if it will expedite the procedure I think that is another reason why we should support it. My hon. friend from Comox-Alberni has proposed an amendment, and I think his suggestion should be adopted. I know several justices of the peace in different parts of the country who are not natural born British subjects, and some of them are located in districts where they would be requested to give certificates to hundreds of foreigners. It would be a tremendous hardship to these people if they had to go to another district in order to obtain that certificate, and this is one reason why I think the amendment suggested by my hon. friend should be supported.

Some hon. members have spoken with regard to the naturalization of people residing in cities, but I say with all respect and deference that any member who knows only the conditions which exist in cities cannot speak authoritatively upon this subject as it affects the country. The ease with which certificates may be secured in a city certainly does not obtain in the country. It has been said that the delay which takes place is not so great, but sometimes it is very long. Occasionally you will find that a judge sits only three times a year; if t'he applicant is unable to attend that court his application may not be heard for six or nine months. Certainly that is a hardship to him, especially if he has to drive twenty-five or thirty miles when the thermometer is forty degrees below zero. Those who have had experience in driving a similar distance under those conditions know that it is a considerable hardship, especially when they are looking forward to something which does not give them very much pleasure.
I was anxious to know what inquiries would be made in connection with these certificates. The leader of the opposition made that a very strong point in his case, and I do not disagree with him at all; I think the inquiries should be as complete as possible. From what I could hear of the statement made to-day by the Secretary of State I understand he proposes to utilize the existing machinery m making these inquiries; that is, it will be done by the mounted police or in some cases by homestead inspectors. From my experience I would say that no better plan can be evolved in the Dominion of Canada. The members of the mounted police are imbued with the esprit de corps and the traditions of their famous force; they make personal calls upon each of the applicants, find out all the circumstances, inquire of the neighbours and make reports which I am sure can be accepted by the Secretary of State as being absolutely correct in almost every particular. Of course you will find the occasional exception, but there is no body in the Dominion of Canada which can so meet the requirements of this act as the mounted police. I know the inquiries they make; they go round the district and ascertain whether or not an applicant is suitable, and I submit that their reports can be relied upon.
The question of language was one of the strongest points in the argument of the leader of the opposition, who said that no application for naturalization should be granted unless the applicant possessed an adequate knowledge of either English or French. I would point out to the leader of the opposition that I have seen men in court who
fMr. Glen.]
could not stand a cross-examination in English. but who would make good citizens. The leader of the opposition directed his question to me personally, and asked if I had never seen in a court of law witnesses who had naturalization papers but who were unable to give their evidence except through an interpreter. Of course I have seen that many times, but I will go further and say that I have seen men in a court obtain their certificates who spoke very halting English. Certainly if these men were to undergo a cross-examination they could not give their evidence without the aid of an interpreter. But I have known of men of this kind who were of excellent character; I know the work they have been doing, the families they have been raising and sending to school, and I know they would make very good citizens of this country. Therefore I would not make that question of language so important that the ability to withstand a cross-examination in court Should be the basis upon which a certificate should be granted. The-mounted police, in reporting on the language qualification, would exercise a good deal of discretion, and I think they may be relied upon. After all, it is not the men coming to this country in the later years of their life who are likely to acquire a fluent knowledge of English; the real reason for naturalization is to assimilate the children into our national life. I think that is the strongest point against the argument of the leader of the opposition, who suggested that a fluent or an adequate knowledge of English must be possessed by an applicant before a certificate can be granted.
I should like to make a Suggestion to the Secretary of State just at this point. In his amendments he is proposing that an applicant for naturalization must advertise his intention in a newspaper published at or nearest to his place of residence. I suggest that in a great many oases the nearest newspaper is published some distance away, and if the amendment could be changed to provide that the advertisement shall be inserted in a newspaper published or circulated at or nearest to his place of residence, I think it would meet the situation better. You would then overcome a difficulty which will be experienced by many applicants. I have already pointed out that if two natural born British subjects certify to the character of the applicant, together with a justice of the peace, who may be natural born or naturalized, that should be sufficient to justify the Secretary of State in granting a certificate of naturalization. If this were granted I should have

no hesitation in supporting this bill in its entirety, satisfied that nothing has been taken away from the act and that a certificate of naturalization will have the same value after these proposed changes as it now has under the present act.

I wish to make a few remarks along a particular line with respect to this bill, but before doing so I want to express my great regret, to put it mildly, at the contemplated change in the act. I think the procedure under the present act is much better, and I regard it as very inadvisable indeed to depart from it, for reasons which have been fully covered by hon. gentlemen on this side of the house. My regret is based on my personal experience in my own constituency, from my observation of the adjoining constituency, and from my judgment generally in the matter.
As to the difficulties that might be encountered in the carrying out of the present act in remote parts of the country, I think they would be amply met by amendment to the present act to provide that judges or other judicial officers, or reputable men selected by the judges, shall visit well recognized centres within striking distance of the settlers generally.
The remarks I wish to make along the particular line relate to the length of residence in Canada in 'connection with repatriation of British born subjects. By section 4, subsection 5 of the present act of 1927, which is the same as section 5, subsection 2 of the former Naturalization Acts of 1914 and 1920, it was provided that the Secretary of State, "in any other special case", might, if he thought fit, grant a certificate of naturalization, although t'he four years' residence or five years' service had not been within the last eight years before the application. By order in council passed on the 4th day of May, 1927, the Secretary of State was empowered to issue special certificates of naturalization to natural born Canadians who, having taken out naturalization papers in the United States of America, had returned to Canada to reside, and that such certificates might be granted after a residence in Canada of one year, the application being made direct to the Secretary of State. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the length of residence should be much less than one year-it should be not more than three months-and that the length of residence should apply not only to natural born Canadians but to British born subjects, who of course in law include natural born Canadians. I submit it would be well
if the minister would provide, by a further addition to his amendment, that the application of natural born British subjects who have been naturalized in the United States should be considered special cases, and that, upon a residence of three months in Canada, such British born subjects could be repatriated.
I quite appreciate Canadian citizenship, with allegiance to the British crown, ought not to be lightly thrown off and lightly assumed again, but we well know that there are hundreds of thousands of Canadian citizens and British subjects living in the United States through unavoidable circumstances, and who long for the day, and are ready at the very earliest opportunity to take advantage oi it, to return to this country again. The love of their native Canada and their love of the empire still bums 'brightly and fervently in their hearts. We should be ready, therefore, to receive them with open arms, and one way of doing that is to provide in the act that when they do come back they may assume their Canadian citizenship and their British allegiance upon a residence of not longer than three months. I would respectfully suggest to the minister that he take that into consideration and add it as an addition to the amendment that he is now bringing in, or as a further amendment to the act.

Several hon.
members on the opposite side of the house have stressed the danger of giving these people naturalization under this newly amended act. One of the supposed dangers is the sixty day clause that is proposed to be put into the act. At present, under the old act, there is stipulated only three months, and the notice of application is posted only in the court house. Under this new act the notice will be advertised in the press, and will be posted in the post office nearest to the applicant's place of residence. Surely, that is far better than placing the notice in the court house, where one is filed on top of the other and in many cases they are seen by only a few7 people.
I do not want to go into the technical or legal side of this question, but in our part of the country it is a matter of great importance. There are thousands of people in that country who would make good citizens and who would like to be naturalized( but it is so difficult for them to become naturalized that they are not becoming Canadian citizens. In the first place they have to go to a court centre and make application

before the clerk of the court; that is one trip. Then an investigation has to be made, and they have to come before the judge again; that is another trip. If the judge happens to have adjourned the court for a certain time, they may have to stay a day or two or they may have to go back. There is so much red tape about becoming naturalized in Canada that thousands of people- who should be naturalized, and who would make good Canadian citizens, are not becoming naturalized.
The impression has been put abroad from this house and from other parts of the country that western Canada is filled with foreigners and undesirable citizens. That is not the case. In the province from which I come, Saskatchewan, we have something over 800,000 people, of whom over 600,000 are British bom.

And of the
195,000 who are not British born, 75,000 were bom in the United States. Our people are a very progressive people and, as a whole, compare favourably with those in any other part of Canada. After all we are endeavouring to build a nation, and I think we have lost sight of the fact that you cannot build a nation in twenty-five or fifty years; it takes much longer than that, as the experience of other nations has shown. These people who are coming to our country are the same people that built the British nation-Norwegians, Swedes, Danes, French, Jutes, Anglos and Saxons. They are the people who are the basic stock of the British. In coming to Great Britain, becoming naturalized and growing up and building the nation they did not make such a bad job of it. After all, the Englishman is a pretty good kind of citizen. I do not see why we should not be ready, under proper safeguards, to naturalize these people and take them into our families. The leader of the opposition in his speech the other day pointed out one or two isolated cases of people in western Canada who had become naturalized and who had not played the game with us during the great war. As reported on page 2551 of Hansard, he said that in -one case a man who had been a German barber in the city of Calgary and who had become a naturalized Canadian citizen -had been seen as a prisoner of war. Then he said:
What did we witness during the war? I wonder if hon. gentlemen recall in their own communities what I have seen in mine.
That may have happened in the case of some of our naturalized citizens, but it would

be much better for the leader of the opposition and everyone else in the house to stress the point that not only hundreds but thousands of these people who were naturalized Canadian citizens or even who were not naturalized, went to France to fight for Canada and many of them laid down their lives for us there. The language qualification is another feature. They must have an adequate knowledge of either English or French. It is right and proper that they should have at least a limited knowledge of either English or French, especially English in the western part of Canada, because in many portions of the west French 'would not be of march use to them.
How would my hon. friend define the word " adequate "?
Everybody who can live in this country for five, ten or fifteen years at peace and do business with his neighbour has possibly an adequate knowledge of the English language.

That may be. In the country from which the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) comes, there are probably half a million people who cannot speak English. There are many people in the north of Scotland who cannot speak English. They speak Gaelic. These aliens are invited to Canada; we give them land; we tell them we will treat them as equals, and yet we put obstacles in their way preventing them from becoming native citizens. Mr. Chairman, I was referring to a remark of the hon. leader of the opposition, that some years ago thousands of people were naturalized in Canada just prior to an election. The fact that those thousands of people were naturalized just prior to an election is perhaps not exactly right, but only because an election was coming on at that time. I do not think there have been any ill effects from having so many of these people naturalized at that time. They

Naturalization Act
have been good citizens of this country, and I have not yet heard any arguments from the opposite side of the house as to why they should not have been naturalized. There should, of course, be certain safeguards, and we should not have an act whereby people could be naturalized just a few days prior to an election.
There is another point. I do not see why we should, put obstacles in the way of people becoming naturalized in this country. If we invite these people into this country; if we bring them here and have them live amongst us for five years or more, mingling with us and their children mingling with our children in the schools, paying taxes, buying made-in-Canada goods, improving and building up our country, I do not see why we should not naturalize them. If they are good enough to live alongside people of this Dominion for five, ten or fifteen years, I think they are good enough to live alongside the people of any place in the British Empire, and I do not see why we should not give them British citizenship.
In the present act surely there are enough safeguards. In the first place, the applicant has to be sponsored by two natural born British citizens and by a justice of the peace. Their record is checked up by the immigration authorities; it is also checked up by the mounted police, and in my opinion that can be done more thoroughly by the police going into the district in which a man has lived for five years than it can be done by any court, because in a great many cases these people are from fifty to one hundred miles away from home when they appear in court, and the court can know very little about them, but on the other hand, the mounted police, going into the district where these people live, can find out all about them in a very short time. I do not see any danger in naturalizing these people. We have found, especially in western Canada, when we take these people into our citizenship, give them responsibility, and let them help us in our community and political life, that they make better citizens; they feel as if they were a part of the country, and they endeavour to do the best they can for the country and for their children who will come after them in this country.
There is one other point, which was touched on by the hon. member for Marquette, and that is that in a great many parts of western Canada it costs far too much to-day to become naturalized. A great many of these people do not know what the regulations are, and they go to a lawyer and they pay from ten, fifteen to twenty, and sometimes fifty dollars to get naturalization. I think we
should make the expense of getting a certificate of naturalization as reasonable as possible, so that we can take more of these people into our citizenship, because they will make good citizens. As I said before, in Saskatchewan we have 195,000 foreign born people, and we find that the children of these people speak and read and write English. Less than 4 per cent of the children in Saskatchewan between ten and twenty years of age, do not read, write and speak the English language. Some of the older people may not be fluent in the English or the French language, but their children learn the language, and so they can really carry on well in the country without a good knowledge of English or French.
I think the government is well advised to put this legislation through. There are thousands of people who will become naturalized very shortly if this legislation goes through. I do not think that my hon. friends opposite need fear at all that the act will be used to naturalize any considerable number of people for the sole purpose of voting in the next election.

I have listened to the discussion in connection with this bill, and while the bill did not suit me very well at first, it is in such a form now as I think will give good satisfaction, and I can support it. Coming from a district where I have an opportunity of judging those who would become naturalized, I think it well to make a few remarks before this bill is voted on.
There seems to be a fear that we may have too large a percentage of our immigration come from the continent. While I am glad to see as many English, Irish and Scotch as we can possibly get, so long as they are physically, mentally and morally suitable, nevertheless, those who come from the continent can make a good contribution. They come from conditions that are a little more difficult even than those encountered in our pioneer life. That tells us one thing: It is quite natural to expect, and we are not surprised when we find, that they can make their way better under those difficult conditions than those of Canadian birth, or those of English, Scotch or Irish birth, who have been raised under a standard of living that is higher and under conditions that are easier.
We have in western Canada considerable land that is second class, and some that we might call third class. Those people who come to us from the continent of Europe, used to a low standard of living, accustomed to work long hours for little pay, by their industry and frugality transform such districts
Naturalization Act

into gardens. I have in mind a settlement where there are 170 families. The land is full of bluffs and sloughs and the percentage of good, arable soil is small. I think it is no reflection on our British immigrants or our Canadian sons to say that very few of them could make both ends meet on that land under the conditions that have obtained during the last ten years. Yet those immigrants from continental Europe have, as I say, turned that district into a garden and constructed good, comfortable houses. They are growing grain and other crops, thus providing freight for the railways and business for the stores. In short, they are valuable assets to this country. It is a mistake to suppose that these people are going to undercut wages. Last spring I saw three fine strapping young fellows. They could not speak a word of English. They had just refused an offer to work at $20 a month, and were standing out for higher wages, even though they required assistance to pay for breakfast. They were advised to accept $20 a month until they had learned the English language. Others have expressed fears that the low standard of living of these people will have a tendenc3' to depress our living standard; but they do not interfere with the farmers around them, they do not tend to lower the standard of living. They are an asset to the community, and I am sure the business men would be very sorry indeed if they left the district. The member for Moose Jaw has well pointed out that in Saskatchewan-where there seems to be the greatest fear that there is too large a proportion of immigration from the continent of Europe-in a population of eight hundred thousand, six hundred thousand are of British birth; that is, many of them may be of foreign parentage, but they were born in Canada or some other British dominion I have seen no sign of real danger that Canadians of British stock are likely to be outnumbered by immigrants of alien birth.
I need not cover the ground already so well covered by the member for Marquette and the member for Moose Jaw and other hon. gentlemen with regard to naturalization. I simply wish to add to what they have said as to the difficulties encountered by the applicant for citizenship. Many of our immigrants would be glad to become naturalized, for they take a pride in British citizenship, and it would be well for Canada to have them naturalized. But when after driving ten, twenty, thirty or forty miles they find the judge is too busy to deal with their applications and they must return a second time, many of these people become discouraged,
[Mr. MillarJ
especially under the conditions that have prevailed during the last few years due to scarcity of money. I think this bill provides all the necessary safeguards. No body of men enjoy to a greater degree the confidence of the people of western Canada than do the Royal Canadian Mounted P,office. They deserve that confidence, and I think they can be trusted to make inquiries of those wishing to become naturalized.

What about homestead
inspectors?
I think my hon. friend ought to have confidence in them because a goodly number were appointed by this party.

I asked for the hon.
gentleman's opinion; I was not expressing my own.

Well, I have considerable confidence in a goodly number of them. I suppose possibly a percentage should be watched, but I believe the great majority of them can be trusted to do the work well. I remember during the war some complaint was made because certain of our immigrants from continental countries with which we were at war did not feel very ready to take up arms in defence of Canada. I admit there is a difficulty in that respect. If I were to go to the United States or any other country, I know I could not throw off my love of Canada in five or even ten years. That is only natural. I would not hold it against an applicant for naturalization if he could not suppress his love for his mother country, and felt uneasy at the prospect that as a Canadian citizen he would have to fight against his native country in the event of war between that country and Canada. If he were not capable of fidelity to the country of his birth he would be a somewhat doubtful citizen of Canada. I think every hon. member would find himself in the same predicament if he became a citizen of another country and that country declared war against his native Canada. It is a difficult situation, but for my part I do not worry very much about it. I am glad the bill has been amended, and I hope it will become law, for under it I am sure we will have many thousands of Canadian citizens applying for naturalization who otherwise would delay for years in some cases. It will be an advantage to Canada to have them naturalized.

Mr. Chairman, when I used to speak more frequently in this house I put myself on record as favouring the admission of thrifty, hard-working people.

Naturalization Act
Some have asked, what about the colour line? Well, I am not so much scared about that as perhaps are some others, because I think our climate will discourage that class from coming here. I aim not in favour of investing so much money to attract immigrants. If I were at the head of the Immigration department I would expatiate on the wonderful possibilities of this vast country for those who are willing to work hard. I am strong for hard work in every department of life. I would say to them: You have the markets of the world for your products. I believe that those who have the energy to come to this country, be their resources little or big, will make good because of their initiative and industry. I am not in favour of inviting sissified, spineless people, people who are living on alms in England, and simlar types. We are spending a vast amount of money in order to promote immigration and to get hand-picked people, so to speak, to come to this country, and it is our bounden duty when they come here to facilitate their becoming naturalized with the least possible delay and with the minimum of cost to themselves. The present bill, in my opinion; alleviates the situation. I am not going to criticize the old law, but I must say that to me it savours somewhat of war time measures. I am not making any accusations against anyone in this regard. I do think however that we should make it easier for people to become naturalized when they are entitled to the privilege. Take the great republic to the south of us. Could that country have been built up to its present proportions if it had enforced a law entailing a good deal of delay and worry and expense to those seeking naturalization? Certainly not. People entered the country without any means at all and they were able to build up wonderful businesses. Some of the greatest men in that country came over carrying all their belongings in a little handkerchief or in a small tin box. There are multitudes' of people in the United States, now good American citizens, who are unable to trace their ancestry to blue blood. The majority of us in Canada can trace our ancestry back to poor people who came to this country in the hope of being able to take advantage of its resources, trusting in those resources and in the laws of the land. Why cannot we enable others now to come and make good?
I submit that we should not withhold the right of the franchise from desirable people. We are now making trade paots throughout the world, and if we pass this law it will be one of the best advertisements to the nations of Canada's greatness. It will be an assurance
to people in all quarters of the globe that, so long as they are fit to come to this country and settle, they will be able to become Canadian citizens without a great deal of delay and expense.
Those who have spoken against this legislation seem to me to have forgotten the brotherhood of man and the fatherhood of God. Do they realize that race hatred and national hatred lead to war? Why should there be any obstacle in the matter of language? People coming from Scotland speak Gaelic and people from Holland speak Dutch; there are a multitude of languages. But why should that debar people from coming to the country? Many people in the middle western states of the American union-fathers and mothers of the present generation-came over with large families, knowing nothing of the language of the country; nor could they learn that language at their age. But their children learned the language and many of them are to-day renowned throughout the United States. I suggest that it would be a good thing for us to trace ourselves back; if we did we should find that we have not sprung from royalty, nor from people born with silver spoons in their mouths.
I submit that this bill should receive the unanimous Support of the house if we are interested in building up this country. Let us have it known throughout the world that Canada is not a country of autocrats, that she is not a country with people who have ideas of race predominance, but that she is ready to welcome all those of good character, those who are willing to work hard and help to build up the country.
It seems to me that it is time to change the present law. The cost of bringing applicants before judges is too great, and the distances they have to travel make it almost impossible for people to become naturalized. Personally I am heartily in favour of the legislation now proposed and I can see no reason whatever for any opposition to it. We need not have any fear of our institutions not being respected if this legislation passes. Let us make it thoroughly understood that this is a country where people must conform to the laws and regulations laid down; let it be known that if a riot should start at any time cold steel will be used if those law3 are not obeyed. Let us see to it that the laws are respected. But I would not withhold the franchise from those worthy of it. There are people who have lived in Canada for years without the franchise although they are fully entitled to it. Why should we put

any obstacle in their way in regard to expense and needless delay ?
I cannot see much reason in any lengthy debate on this question. People outside are looking to see what we are going to do with this legislation which is now before the committee. Immigration and naturalization are linked together so closely that if we refuse to pass this measure it will be heralded abroad, "You may go to Canada if you like, but you will never become naturalized/' The Americans have never kept people out of the United States in that way. Canadians go there and find no difficulty in becoming naturalized if they wish to become citizens of the United States. Let us also make it easier for desirable people to become naturalized in Canada. Let us do everything in conformity with the forward step which we are taking in Canada in other directions. It does not seem to me that this measure calls for any lengthy debate and I shall therefore not weary the committee longer.

I have listened with
a good deal of interest to the discussion of the proposed amendments, a discussion which has been very instructive. I appreciate very much indeed the effort the Secretary of State made to enlighten the house on the whole question of naturalization. The leader of the opposition also gave the house much valuable information, which no doubt many of us lacked before we had the privilege of hearing him. My first word is this: If these amendments are likely to bring back the conditions that existed in this country prior to the passing of the act in 1914 I am absolutely opposed to them. I remember the conditions that prevailed in Saskatchewan in my early homesteading experience. In my judgment nothing would deter people coming to this country from thinking well of the country so much as the manner in which certificates were issued for naturalization, particularly around election time. I have known government officials to have their pockets full of these certificates all ready to hand out to those who were willing to promise their support to the particular candidate of those officials. If these amendments are going to bring back, even in part, such a condition as that then I think this house should be very careful before going further with them.
The Secretary of State in stating his case was asked the question 'how evidence would be secured as to whether an alien should be granted a certificate. He said that the mounted police, the homestead inspectors and other persons would be in a position to secure that evidence. So far as the mounted police

are concerned, I would not object to them, but when we come down to the homestead inspectors and other persons I say we should draw the line night there. We are not told who the other persons are to be, but in my judgment the homestead inspectors have been responsible in the past for many hardships which were suffered by aliens coming to this country. In my judgment there are only two reasons which might be advanced for changing the present act, and the first of these is that the present act must be unworkable. I have not heard as yet any good argument advanced to show that the act is unworkable; certainly it is not so in the cities, where it is quite easy for any person to go before a judge and make application for a naturalization certificate. When we come to the outlying portions of the country there is a possibility that there may be some hardship in a few cases, but amendments might be made to provide for such cases. Since I have been a member of this house I have represented two large but very thinly populated constituencies, in which many people live forty or fifty miles from a railway centre, and I have never heard one complaint of inability to secure naturalization certificates. As I have already said, in some sections of the country with which I am not familiar there may be the possibility of hardship, but without tearing the act to pieces it should be possible to provide for such cases.
The only other reason which could be put forward for these amendments is that politicians desire to secure the naturalization of large numbers of aliens for the purpose of securing their votes. I would suggest to the house that it is not advisable even for political purposes to place ourselves in the position of allowing an alien to look lightly upon naturalization in this country. We hold Canadian citizenship in high regard because of the fact that we not only make a man a Canadian citizen; he also becomes a citizen of the British Empire, and to that extent we have a responsibility to other parts of the empire.
The Secretary of State has also made the excuse that some of the judges claim to be incapable of interpreting the Naturalization Act. If the judges are not capable of interpreting that act and of forming an opinion as to whether a person is fit to become a Canadian citizen and a British subject, how would the minister expect a mounted policeman, a homestead inspector or any other person to be able to interpret the act? I think that argument is very faulty, and it defeats the very object the Secretary of State has in view. I would also remind the committee that we have a special committee of

this house sitting to go into the question of whether the salaries of our judges should be increased, and I think probably the government are behind this proposal. This statement by the Secretary of State does not appeal to me as a very strong argument for increasing the salaries of our judges.
I am not going to take up the time of the committee further except to say a few words with regard to the amendments, the first of which improved the original amendment to a great extent; I refer to the provision for posting notices for sixty days. That removes some objections to the proposed amendments, but I should be much more satisfied if the Secretary of State would agree to an extension of that time to four or six months. Let us make this provision such that we can say in good faith that because of the time required for the posting of notices no political party can benefit by this act at election time. If we put it on that basis I think probably the house and the country will be more satisfied with the proposal than is the case at the present. Provision is also made for objections to such applications, but in this amendment the Secretary of State has not said where these objections are to be lodged. In my judgment that is a grave omission. Under the present act a person who objects to an application for naturalization can appear in court and present his objection before the judge and the person concerned. Therefore I think some provision should be made whereby persons objecting to a naturalization application should send their protests to the Secretary of State, where they will be given proper consideration.
The only other reference I wish to make is with regard to the three natural bom British subjects who are to give a certificate of character. I do not look upon that part of the section as being very strong; in fact it has an inherent weakness. If it is possible when these amendments are passed-if they are passed-for a political party to take advantage of the situation during election time, it is possible for a party to get as many British bom subjects as may be required to give certificates of character. Consequently that is not a very strong safeguard. I think the greatest safeguard we can have either now or in the future is to see that sufficient time elapses between the filing of the application and the final granting of the certificate so that no political party can take advantage of this act.

Before this bill passes I should like to make a few observations, although I do not intend to delay the committee very long. I think the government
and the Secretary of State are to be congratulated for bringing this bill 'before the house. I have lived in western Canada most of my life and have come in contact with a good many men from European countries. I have found that many of them have had difficulty in becoming British subjects, and to my mind this difficulty should be removed. If we are going to make it as hard as possible for a man to become a citizen of Canada I think our whole immigration policy will fall to pieces.
